title: Guitarist Louis Gonzales and the Strayhorn arrangements
summary: Lee explains his violinist-turned-guitarist school friend could read single-line parts, so Strayhorn, Wilson and Brooks wrote four-part arrangements, including a condensed Flamingo.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: What happened to Louis Gonzales? You said he was playing guitar parts in your band, right?
And that was somewhat unusual, because most guitarists were still playing rhythm, weren't they?

Yeah. Well, that was -- the object of it -- that was why I think I also stated that Billy Strayhorn and Gerald Wilson and Dudley Brooks were making our arrangements. Well, this was why they were making the arrangements, because we had 2 tenors, a trumpet and a guitar,

and they wrote 4 part harmony for them. And then with the amplification -- when you turned the amplifier on and with the bottom with the 2 tenors and the trumpet and the guitar, it was really a great sound, you know. And incidentally, Louis was in the band in junior high school together; we went to school together.
What happened to him after your band?
Because I never heard his name before.

Oh no. He played Los Angeles a lot. He was, first he was a violin player, you know, and then he started playing guitar; that's why we were not afraid to write the parts for him, you see, because he was a violinist, so during that era, there wasn't that many guitar players, I don't think, that could read single string, you know, but he could -- because he was a violinist, and that's why it worked all right.
But no, he kind of dropped out of music. He was married and I think he had about 7 or 8 kids. But he dropped out of music.
Do you still have those arrangements by Strayhorn and Wilson and Brooks?
Oh, I would think I probably have,

because Billy made arrangements for us on Flamingo -- made the identical same arrangements they had, and he condensed it so our four instruments could play it, and we started the same way they did, and you know, he was pretty sharp as a writer.
Wasn't that his first arrangement for Duke? The vocal arrangement of "Flamingo"?
I don't really know. Now, you would know that better than I would.
I think that's what Duke told me. Now Duke said it was the renaissance of vocal arranging when he wrote it.
